title: Optimizing LLM Serving Efficiency: Moving Beyond KV Cache Reuse to Token-Load Awareness with Ray Serve LLM | Anyscale
gist: Anyscale argues that optimizing LLM-serving routers purely for KV cache reuse is a mistake -- it causes 'request herding' and load imbalance under heterogeneous, multi-turn traffic -- and introduces KVAwareRouter, which trades some cache-hit rate for token-load balance and wins on p99 rollout latency in synthetic RL benchmarks and on TTFT/TPOT/throughput when replayed against real Claude Code agent traces.

themes.theme: Contrarian thesis: KV cache reuse alone is the wrong routing objective

insights.claim: Maximizing KV cache reuse is explicitly framed as 'the most naive approach' to LLM serving optimization: it does not necessarily maximize actual serving performance, because it ignores how work is actually distributed across replicas once caching decisions are made.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wang et al.
insights.so_what: Directly challenges what the article calls the industry's default optimization target for LLM routers -- relevant to anyone evaluating or building vLLM-fleet routing logic, including in-house router implementations at other labs.
insights.locator: Why Isn't Maximizing KV Cache Reuse Alone Enough?

insights.claim: Pure KV-cache-affinity routing causes 'request herding': once a replica caches a shared prefix such as a common system prompt, subsequent unrelated requests from many different conversations all see cache overlap and preferentially route to that same replica, creating token-load imbalance even though each individual routing decision looked locally optimal.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wang et al.
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, non-obvious failure mode of cache-affinity routing that is easy to miss when evaluating routers on cache-hit-rate metrics alone.

insights.claim: Session affinity via consistent hashing balances the number of sessions evenly across replicas but treats all sessions as equal weight, so it has no visibility into a session containing a long-running straggler turn -- multiple stragglers can land on the same replica and create load imbalance despite an evenly distributed request count.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wang et al.
insights.so_what: Shows that even a load-balancing-aware routing scheme (consistent hashing) can fail on real workloads because it balances the wrong unit (session count, not actual compute load).

themes.theme: Token load as the corrected routing objective

insights.claim: The corrected framing treats KV cache overlap as an input to load *estimation* rather than the routing objective itself: the real objective, 'token load,' combines remaining prefill work (uncached input tokens) plus ongoing decode work from active requests into a single per-replica metric.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wang et al.
insights.so_what: A generalizable reframing of the LLM-serving routing problem that other serving-infrastructure teams (in-house at labs, or competing router vendors) could adopt or need to differentiate against.
insights.locator: Beyond KV Cache Reuse: Token Load Awareness Matters More

insights.claim: KVAwareRouter ingests live KV-cache-block events emitted directly by vLLM (via an integration with NVIDIA Dynamo's KV indexer) to build a global radix tree, giving it both an up-to-date view of cache overlap and automatic KV cache reuse discovery without requiring clients to supply explicit session IDs, unlike consistent-hashing session affinity.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wang et al.
insights.so_what: Notable cross-vendor technical collaboration (Anyscale/Ray Serve with NVIDIA's Dynamo team) on a shared serving-routing component -- relevant to assessing NVIDIA's broader software-stack influence over inference orchestration.
insights.locator: Beyond KV Cache Reuse: Token Load Awareness Matters More

insights.claim: Router state is only eventually consistent across replicas by design: KVAwareRouter makes routing decisions locally then asynchronously shares load updates with peer routers, deliberately keeping synchronization off the token-streaming hot path in exchange for a slightly stale global load view.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wang et al.
insights.locator: Beyond KV Cache Reuse: Token Load Awareness Matters More

themes.theme: Controlled experiment: asynchronous multi-turn RL rollouts

insights.claim: In a synthetic asynchronous RL rollout benchmark (8 rollouts per step, 10 turns each, with 2 straggler turns generating 8K tokens versus a normal 1K), KVAwareRouter achieves the best p99 end-to-end rollout latency among the three tested routers despite having a lower prefix-cache hit rate than the router optimized purely for cache affinity -- an explicit, measured trade of cache reuse for load balance.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wang et al.
insights.so_what: A clean, controlled demonstration that the lower-cache-hit-rate router wins on the metric that actually matters (p99 latency/step time) for asynchronous RL training loops -- directly useful for anyone running large-scale RL rollout infrastructure.
insights.locator: Why Isn't Maximizing KV Cache Reuse Alone Enough?

themes.theme: Real-world validation on Claude Code agent traces

insights.claim: Replaying a filtered subset of real Weka Claude Code agent traces (sized to fit gpt-oss-120b's context window) shows extreme session heterogeneity: some sessions are single-turn while others span dozens of turns and accumulate millions of input tokens, which the authors present as the realistic regime where naive cache-affinity routing fails.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wang et al.
insights.so_what: Establishes that coding-agent traffic specifically (not generic chat) is the heterogeneous, high-variance workload class that breaks simple routing heuristics -- a directly relevant data point as agentic coding tools scale in production serving volume.
insights.locator: Case Study: Replaying Claude Code Traces

insights.claim: On this real Claude Code trace replay, KVAwareRouter outperforms session affinity with consistent hashing on TTFT, TPOT, and throughput, while prefix-cache hit rate is shown to drop for all routers as concurrency increases -- demonstrating that pure cache-based routing degrades precisely as load scales up, which is exactly when serving efficiency matters most.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wang et al.
insights.so_what: Validates the token-load-aware approach on production-like agentic traffic rather than only synthetic benchmarks, and flags cache-eviction-under-load as a real-world confound that any cache-affinity-based router must contend with at scale.
insights.locator: Case Study: Replaying Claude Code Traces

insights.claim: Non-deterministic output length remains an explicitly unsolved problem: because generation length is unknown at request admission time, requests that initially look lightweight can still turn into long decode-phase stragglers and create unexpected token-load imbalance, with agentic harnesses providing generation-length hints proposed as one possible (not-yet-existing) mitigation.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wang et al.
insights.so_what: An honest acknowledgment that token-load-aware routing does not fully solve the routing problem -- an open gap that any competing router (or future Ray Serve LLM release) will need to address, and a potential product opportunity for agentic frameworks to expose generation-length hints.

insights.claim: Session affinity via consistent hashing is still recommended over KVAwareRouter in narrower cases: when cache misses are especially expensive (very long multi-turn chat), when cross-session cache reuse is limited (sessions diverge quickly after a shared prompt), or when sessions have homogeneous workloads -- meaning KVAwareRouter is positioned as a workload-dependent choice, not a strict universal replacement.
insights.speaker: Jeffrey Wang et al.
insights.so_what: Important nuance for practitioners: the 'better' router depends on workload shape, so a one-size-fits-all router choice risks leaving performance on the table in either direction.
insights.locator: Beyond KV Cache Reuse: Token Load Awareness Matters More
